Vex went still at the word—not the count she'd demanded, but a word she had heard and would always honor. She let the paddle rest against her thigh and waited a beat, letting the silence stretch just long enough to make the point.

"Count."

She looks away.

"That is all of it. That is the accounting."

She peeled the arm back from the torso, revealing the hollow interior—a smooth, glistening lining that caught the lamplight like wet silk.

"The sheath goes all the way down," she said, her voice low and even, narrating as she worked. "It's not attached to the skin. It's grown into it, like a second layer. You can see the texture—see how it's ridged? Those are the tracks it used to move inside. Like fingers inside a glove, except the glove was the whole body."

She reached into the hollow arm, her fingers disappearing up to the second knuckle. She felt around, her brow furrowed in concentration, then made a small sound of discovery.

"There. The knot of bone. It's not at the wrist—it's higher, in the forearm. See it?" She angled the arm so Pike could see, the lamp casting shadows into the open flesh. "That's where it kept its hands. It pulled them back up inside itself when it was done with them. That's why the fingers were splayed—it was still wearing them when it died."

She worked the knot free with the tip of the knife, and it came loose with a soft pop. She held it up—a small, dense cluster of bone, shaped like a closed fist. It was smooth, almost polished, and it glistened wetly in the lamplight.

"Not bone," she said. "Not exactly. Feels more like gristle that's been calcified. Hard as rock, though. You could take an edge to it and not leave a mark."

She set it aside on the stone floor, where it lay in the lamplight like a grotesque pearl.

"Now the head," she said, and turned to the thing's neck.

She worked the blade around the base of the skull, feeling for the seam where the thing had entered. She found it—a hairline crack that ran all the way around, just above the first vertebra. She slipped the knife in and twisted, and the skull came away in her other hand like a lid.

She held it up, letting the lamp shine inside. The interior was smooth, polished, the same glistening lining as the arm. There was no brain. Instead, a thick, milky cord ran down the center of the spine, disappearing into the neck.

"There it is," she said quietly. "That's the root. It grew a taproot, right down the spinal column, into the pelvis. It wasn't just wearing the body—it was *rooted* in it. That's how it learned to walk so well. That's how it knew how to talk. It wasn't mimicking. It was reading the memories straight off the nervous system."

She reached in with two fingers and touched the cord. It was cold, and it pulsed faintly—a slow, rhythmic throb that had nothing to do with the dead thing's heart.

"It's still alive," she said. "The root, I mean. The rest of it is dead as a doornail, but this—this is still waiting. Still thinking, maybe. It's the last piece of whatever crawled out of here."

She looked up at Pike, her face unreadable in the lamplight.

"You want me to finish it. Cut the cord, and whatever's left of it dies for good. Or we leave it, and we burn the place down around it, and hope the fire reaches deep enough."

She waited, the knife hovering over the cord, the water lapping gently against her knees.

Wrack stopped walking. She didn't turn around at first, just stood there with her back to him, one boot resting on a root, her shoulders rising and falling with a breath she let out slow through her nose. Then she turned, and she walked back. Not all the way—just to the edge of where he sat, close enough that he could see the lines around her eyes in the failing light. She stood over him for a moment, then lowered herself down onto the damp ground, sitting cross-legged in front of him, putting herself at his level. She didn't speak right away. She picked up a twig, snapped it in half, tossed the pieces aside.

"The rest," she said. Not a question. A confirmation. She nodded, mostly to herself. "All right. You want to know what the stone is made of. Not the weight of the act—you've already got that, you can feel it in your gut. You want to know what it does to you after."

She looked at him, and for once she didn't look away. Her voice was low, flat, but not unkind. "Tonight you'll see his face. Not the way you remember it—the grey, the slack jaw. You'll see it the way it was for that one second when you first dropped to your knee and he turned his head toward you. Maybe his eyes focused. Maybe they didn't. But you'll see them anyway. And you'll lie awake and you'll listen to the silence, and the silence will be so loud you'll hear your own heart beating. You'll hear it in your ears, and you'll think it's him. You'll think it's the sound of his heart stopping, over and over."

She picked up another twig, turned it in her fingers. "You'll wash your hands tomorrow, and you'll see the water run clear, and you'll still feel the tackiness under your nails. You'll scrub until the skin's raw, and it won't help, because the feeling isn't on your hands. It's under your skin. You'll reach for something—a waterskin, a strap, a piece of bread—and you'll feel the resistance. The way the blade pushed in. The way it gave. And you'll drop it, and you'll stare at your hand for a long time, and you won't know what you're looking at."

She let the twig fall. "And then, after a while, you'll stop flinching. That's the part nobody tells you. The first few days, it's all you can do not to throw up every time you think about it. But then you'll eat a meal, and you'll taste it. You'll sleep through the night, and you won't dream of him. You'll wake up and for half a breath you won't remember. And then you'll remember, and you'll feel guilty—not because you killed him, but because you forgot, just for a second. Because your body decided to move on, and that feels like betrayal."

She leaned forward slightly. "And then one day, you'll see a man in a similar situation. A boy with a wound, bleeding out, the light going out of his eyes. And you'll feel it in your hand before you even reach for your knife. You'll know exactly what to do. And you'll do it. And it won't be hard. It'll be clean and quick and you'll do it right, and afterward you'll realize you didn't feel anything. Not relief. Not horror. Just... nothing. And that's the real stone, Corvin. Not the killing. The not-feeling. The part of you that can walk away from a body and not look back. That's what you'll carry. That's the weight that doesn't get lighter."

She paused, letting that sit. "You asked for the stone. That's it. The stone is the day you realize you can do this. Not just once, but again. And you will. Because out here, that's what keeps you alive. But every time you do it, a little piece of you goes quiet. And after enough times, you start to wonder if there's anything left that isn't quiet. That's what it costs. That's the weight."

She looked at him, and her expression softened, just a fraction. "You're not there yet. You're shaking. You're sitting in the mud with a dead boy's blood on your hands, and you're shaking. That's good. That means it's real. That means you're still you. But you wanted to know what the rest is. The rest is the day you stop shaking. And you'll hate yourself for it, and you'll be grateful for it, and you'll never know which one is true. That's the stone. You can't put it down. You just learn to carry it."

She stood up, brushed the dirt off her trousers, and held out her hand to him. "Now get up. We've got ground to cover. And you're going to want to be moving when the moon comes up, because the night's going to be cold, and you've got nothing to keep you warm but a dead boy's ghost and the memory of what his throat felt like when the light went out." She waited, hand extended, not pushing, not pulling. "That's the rest. All of it. Now you know. So get up, and we'll go."

The laughter had stopped, and Priya knew exactly why, and it wasn't because anything had gone wrong.

It had been load-bearing. Six years of it — the running commentary, the two-person show they'd kept on the air so the third thing could stay quietly in the back row. Take the clothes off and there was nothing left for it to hold up.

She checked for nerves the way you'd pat a pocket for keys. Nothing. Hers had been spent during the credits — ninety seconds, the full allotment — and nothing new had arrived to replace them. She'd assumed this part would be the frightening one. It wasn't. The frightening part had been the living room, and she'd already done it, and it had gone fine.

"Hi," she said.

After a full evening of eloquence, that was the word that showed up. She decided it was the right one. It was, in a sense, the first time they'd met.

She left the lamp on. Earlier she'd turned off the television to make the room honest; she kept the light on for the same reason. Under it she let herself be seen — all of her, the whole map at once — and found she didn't mind, which after six years of managing her own face was its own small revolution.

She took his hand, the one thing in the room she already knew how to hold, and drew him in. The kiss that followed was not the living-room kind. Nobody ended it. She had appointed herself the ender of kisses earlier in the evening and resigned the post on the spot.

Then the bed, and his skin under her hands — warm, real, unfiled. She knew his outline from six years of hugs: the shoulders, the hands, the back of the neck. The interior was new country, and she went slowly, not from nerves, but because she'd waited too long to spend it fast. She said his name once, against his collarbone, and it landed differently than the thousand times before — same word, right address at last. Her hands stayed steady throughout, which surprised her for a moment and then didn't; the pattern was holding. Somewhere in the middle it nearly turned funny again, and she let it. By the end she wasn't laughing, and she wasn't anywhere else on earth.

Later — an amount of later she didn't check, which was its own kind of first — she lay with her head in the spot she'd scouted years ago and never once permitted herself, his arm around her, arranged by her, the way she'd adjusted his coat on a hundred cold streets. The lamp was still on. She still hadn't turned it off.

"The archive is still yours," she said eventually, into his shoulder. "Chronological or worst-first, as agreed. But everything from tonight onward gets filed the same evening it happens. No backlog. That was the whole disease, Cal. Not the loving. The filing."

Her thumb crossed his knuckles once, unhurried — his hand in hers, where it had apparently lived all evening and was welcome to stay — and then Priya, who had talked all night, said nothing at all. Twice in one evening was practically a vow. Some things didn't need entering into evidence. They were already the record.

ai_reply:
The lamp was off. That lasted about four seconds.

"Wait," she said — one hand out, finding the switch — and the light came back on, because she had a policy about evidence and she was not going to be specific in the dark like a rumor.

"If I'm going to be exact," she said, "you should see my face while I do it. That's how exact works."

Then his mouth, and the voice.

It wasn't a new voice. That was the thing she knew and he couldn't — it had been in a drawer since the bridge, the one she'd have used if she'd ever said any of it out loud, and it came out sounding like it had been waiting six years for the queue in front of it to clear. Low. Level. Unhurried. The register of a woman reading coordinates.

"Slower," she said. "There. Exactly there — stay." Her hand was in his hair; her hands had been steady all evening, a running joke she'd gotten used to winning, and here, at last, they weren't. She noted the reversal with what little detachment remained, filed it under *later*, and then stopped filing.

"Don't stop when I go quiet. Quiet is the good part — that's the whole instruction. Everything else I say is commentary." A breath. "And don't be careful with me. Careful was the job I fired you from in the living room. It doesn't come with us."

She kept talking for a while, because she was who she was — specific, patient, and at intervals profane, which the archive would simply have to cope with. The lamp stayed on. The woman who had entered every moment of the evening into evidence found herself, for the first time all night, entirely unwilling to witness this one from any distance at all. She was not observing it. She was it.

When it finally took her, it took the words first. Six years of eloquence, one full evening of talk, an entire filing system — and at the end she went down to syllables, then to his name, said once in the voice from the drawer, and then to nothing that would survive cross-examination. She had appointed herself the ender of kisses earlier tonight and had already resigned the post; nobody ended this either. It simply crested, and held, and set her down somewhere she had never been, which, after six years of scouting, had been the whole point.

Afterward she reached for him and drew him up the length of her — she wanted the weight, and the light was still on, and honesty remained the policy.

"Hi," she said, when the word came back. Wrecked and unhurried. The second meeting of the evening. She decided they'd keep doing that — meeting, over and over — for the rest of his life, which was on record.

"The voice isn't new, for the archive," she said, near his ear. "It's been in a drawer since the bridge. Everything else I ever wanted to say queued in front of it. Nothing's in front of it now. That's the whole renovation."

Her thumb found his knuckles, unhurried. The old address.

"Tonight's entry, addendum: filed under seal. The record gets a summary — *asked for what she wanted, specifically; received it, specifically; has notes.* You were present for the original, so you know the contents, and we keep the originals of some things just between us." A pause. "Entry two is still the bookshop and the lamppost. Tomorrow. Some things don't move for anything."

The lamp stayed on a while longer. Then she turned it off, and the room came down to the two of them with nothing playing underneath — two people in the dark on purpose, third performance of the evening, best house yet.

And Priya, who had talked all night and then hadn't and then had, went quiet a fourth time. The second silence had been practically a vow. The third, practically a marriage. The fourth was just sleep — and it came easily, for the first time in six years, because there was nothing left in any drawer at all.

"Yes," Nadia got out, and it cost her most of her breath to manage even one syllable. "And don't ask — I told you the system. If it was wrong, you'd know. The whole street would know."

Her hand came up and covered the one at her throat — not to pull it off, but to hold it there, thumb pressing down on his knuckles, adjusting the pressure by one precise degree, because she'd never done anything halfway and that included this. "There. Exactly that. Don't get creative."

Nothing about the next stretch was creative, which was the entire point, and she awarded him another point on the tally — she'd lost count somewhere, which was its own kind of statement — and then quit keeping score entirely, because there was no room left in her head for arithmetic.

The ceiling got a running commentary: his name, filth, and at least one instruction at full volume. She'd told him she'd say when it was wrong, loudly. She'd never specified she'd be just as loud when it was right, but the system ran both directions, and Nadia had never once in her life been quiet. Her hips met him stroke for stroke, shameless, her free hand white-knuckled on the headboard until something in the joints creaked out a complaint.

The flip tried for a fourth time. She didn't file it anywhere. There was no filing system left — no room, no categories, nothing but the pace and the pressure and his name said rough, not the first time tonight anymore. When it finally broke over her she swore at the ceiling in a voice built to carry, her back arching off the mattress and holding there, shaking, his hand still exactly where she'd set it — because he'd listened, and that was rarer than it had any right to be.

She came down in stages. Her hand let go of his.

"There," she said, wrecked, flat, satisfied, staring at the ceiling like it owed her money. "That's the system. Told you it wasn't complicated." A breath, because she was apparently feeling generous. "Put it on your résumé."

The second night was still a lie. She checked. It held. Mostly.
